network.overall_strategy: Construct the experimentally resolved cyanosulfidic proline-aminonitrile scaffold, evaluate three explicitly proposed hydrolysis regimes, and retain four additional experimentally reported proline-producing reaction families as empirical synthesis-and-recovery modules. The ten pathway entries are distinct reaction sequences, not ten independently demonstrated synthesis mechanisms: P1-P3 begin with supplied HCN, P4-P6 explicitly generate that HCN by atmospheric discharge, and P7-P10 represent four additional scaffold-producing families. None establishes L-selectivity. L-proline is represented as an expected component of a DL mixture, with D-proline explicitly included; no unsupported resolution step is invented. Reaction records distinguish reported observations from proposed operating windows and unresolved environmental integration. Reference equations in mechanism fields specify atom-balanced bookkeeping, not measured product distributions or yields. S8 represents an idealized zero-valent sulfur sink, while formic acid in two empirical modules is an unverified oxidized-carbon balancing product. Neither assignment establishes the actual coproduct inventory. Neutral molecular formulas represent acid-base pools: actual solutions contain condition-dependent cyanide, hydrosulfide, ammonium, formate and proline ionic species. The schema lacks a coproduct role, so terminal coproducts use intermediate. A null environment_formed denotes external supply or formation in multiple environments. Pressurized experiments above 370 K are assigned to Hydrothermal as thermal-environment analogues, not misrepresented as ambient-pressure surface experiments. Extraterrestrial ice and irradiated-formamide experiments are excluded because their demonstrated conditions do not fit the requested terrestrial settings. This is a connected, evidence-graded research network, not a demonstrated autonomous geochemical synthesis of purified L-proline.

reactions.name: Copper-assisted hydrocyanation of acetylene

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K; proposed operating screen, not a quoted experimental optimum
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar, with replenished gas-liquid contact
conditions.other: Anoxic, initially dark gas-contacting pool. Proposed screening concentrations: 10-50 mM total HCN/CN-, 1-20 mM dissolved acetylene, and 10-100 micromolar total copper; pH 7-8.5. Screen hours to one day. Introduce sulfide only downstream because copper sulfide precipitation can remove the catalyst. Retention of volatile HCN and acetylene is an unresolved field requirement.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-mediated addition of HCN across the acetylene triple bond forms acrylonitrile. Reference balance: mol_002 + mol_003 -> mol_007.
reactions.reasoning: Supported transformation: Patel et al. (2015) connect HCN/acetylene chemistry to the acrylonitrile entry of the proline branch. Copper is assigned a coordination-catalytic role, not a generic mineral-surface role. The numerical operating screen above is proposed here rather than presented as the published protocol. A naturally available, soluble copper-cyanide pool and staged exclusion of sulfide remain environmental bottlenecks; detection of copper minerals alone would not establish catalytic availability.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 9-10, 1-30 mM acrylonitrile and 0.1-1 M total ammonia/ammonium, with ammonia in excess; hours to one day. Keep dark and add sulfide only after this stage. Excess ammonia and limited acrylonitrile availability are intended to suppress repeated cyanoethylation, but their natural attainment is not established.

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia to the terminal carbon of acrylonitrile gives 3-aminopropanenitrile. Reference balance: mol_007 + mol_004 -> mol_008.
reactions.reasoning: Supported transformation: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 83% conversion in their tested segment. That value is not assigned to the proposed concentration and pH window or to an environmental reactor. Overaddition and competing polymerization can divert material, and the ammonia-rich stage cannot simply be assumed compatible with all subsequent reactions.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.catalyst: Copper-cyanide photoredox pool; its substrate-specific contribution requires verification
conditions.other: Proposed screen: 1-20 mM aminonitrile, 5-100 mM total dissolved sulfide, 10-100 micromolar copper, pH 7-8.5, and UV within the short-wavelength surface-accessible spectrum. A 254 nm laboratory source is a reference test, not a demonstrated solar dose. Sample over approximately 0.5-12 hours and capture the aminoaldehyde promptly. Measure dissolved copper and sulfide because copper sulfide precipitation can suppress catalysis.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical reducing equivalents supplied by sulfide reduce the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases 3-aminopropanal and ammonia. Formal sulfur-endmember balance: 8 mol_008 + 8 mol_005 + 8 mol_001 -> 8 mol_009 + 8 mol_004 + mol_006. S8 represents an oxidized sulfur reservoir, not an established exclusive photoproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Supported substrate transformation: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 45% conversion to beta-aminopropionaldehyde in an optimized segment. This network does not introduce a supposedly validated copper-free alternative for this particular substrate. Copper is included in the proposed implementation, but the supplied summary does not establish its separate quantitative benefit at the stated concentrations. Sulfide is a consumed reductant, not merely an agent. Sulfur speciation, aldehyde lifetime, UV dose and achievable environmental throughput remain unclosed.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin capture of 3-aminopropanal

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 6.5-8, freshly generated aminoaldehyde at 1-20 mM and one to five molar equivalents of total cyanide; minutes to hours in a shaded receiving microenvironment. Transfer promptly from irradiation and avoid prolonged storage of the free aminoaldehyde. No quantitative purification from residual ammonia, copper or sulfide is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by proton transfer, producing 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanenitrile. Reference balance: mol_009 + mol_002 -> mol_010. The new stereocenter is not assigned an enantiomeric preference.
reactions.reasoning: Supported transformation: Patel et al. (2015) report essentially quantitative cyanohydrin formation under their tested conditions. That observation supports rapid capture as a chemically meaningful operation, but does not demonstrate the proposed transfer or concentration window. Aminoaldehyde oligomerization and competing imine chemistry must be assessed in the actual preceding reaction mixture.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to the aminoaldehyde cyanohydrin nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-9, 1-20 mM cyanohydrin and 5-100 mM total sulfide; monitor over hours to days. Use a shaded compartment for the addition stage before the later irradiation step. Sulfide is a stoichiometric sulfur reagent here.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide addition to the nitrile followed by proton transfer and tautomerization generates the alpha-hydroxythioamide manifold. Reference balance: mol_010 + mol_005 -> mol_011.
reactions.reasoning: Supported reaction manifold: Patel et al. (2015) describe cyanohydrin-derived alpha-hydroxythioamides en route to cyclic thioamides. This node represents the structurally relevant connectivity, not proof that a single pure thioamide accumulates exclusively or is isolated at this stage. The proposed pH, concentrations and residence times require substrate-specific testing.

reactions.name: Five-membered thiolactam ring formation

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9 and millimolar hydroxythioamide, monitored over 1-48 hours. Test lower-ammonia aliquots rather than assuming that the ammonia-rich mixture from rxn_002 cyclizes equally efficiently. Exchange, dilution or prior ammonia loss would need to occur without losing the organic substrate; no automatic environmental separation is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal amino group attacks the thioamide carbon intramolecularly. Elimination of ammonia produces the five-membered alpha-hydroxythiolactam. Reference balance: mol_011 -> mol_012 + mol_004.
reactions.reasoning: Supported ring-construction logic: Patel et al. (2015) identify formation and cyclization within the hydroxythioamide manifold. Five-membered ring closure supplies the structural operation missing from an ordinary acyclic Strecker synthesis. The separate node is a mechanistic decomposition of that manifold, not a claim that every intermediate was independently isolated or that ammonia removal has been demonstrated in a natural pool.

reactions.name: Photoreductive deoxygenation to gamma-butyrothiolactam

conditions.catalyst: Copper-cyanide photoredox pool, included as a proposed implementation rather than asserted to be universally necessary
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-8.5, 1-20 mM cyclic hydroxythioamide, 10-100 mM total sulfide and 10-100 micromolar copper. Apply UV in a thin water layer and follow substrate loss and thiolactam formation during an initial 0.5-12 hour dose screen. Limit continued exposure after product accumulation.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-supported photoreduction removes the alpha-hydroxyl functionality while retaining the thiolactam ring. Formal sulfur-endmember balance: 8 mol_012 + 8 mol_005 -> 8 mol_013 + 8 mol_001 + mol_006.
reactions.reasoning: Supported transformation sequence: Patel et al. (2015) connect the cyclic hydroxythioamide manifold to gamma-butyrothiolactam by irradiation/reduction. The proposed copper-containing operating window is not a claim of a published catalyst-omission comparison for this substrate. Product selectivity and sulfur speciation must be measured; the S8 balance does not demonstrate that pure cyclooctasulfur is the actual sole oxidation product.

reactions.name: Thiolactam photoreduction followed by cyanide trapping

conditions.catalyst: Copper-cyanide photoredox pool in the reduction stage
conditions.other: Two-stage operation: first irradiate millimolar thiolactam with a proposed 10-100 mM sulfide pool at pH 7-8.5; then limit irradiation and provide cyanide for trapping. Screen one to five cyanide equivalents during trapping rather than assuming arbitrary simultaneous mixing is equivalent. Copper solubility, UV dose, sulfide availability and the timing of cyanide exposure must be verified experimentally.

reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction/desulfurization accesses a transient cyclic imine or its aqueous precursor, followed by cyanide capture to form pyrrolidine-2-carbonitrile. The transient imine is not asserted to be an independently isolated compound. Formal sulfur-endmember balance: 8 mol_013 + 8 mol_002 + 8 mol_005 -> 8 mol_014 + 8 mol_005 + mol_006. Sulfide appears on both sides because donor oxidation and substrate desulfurization can consume and regenerate sulfide pools; this is not evidence of quantitative reductant recycling.
reactions.reasoning: Supported immediate-precursor endpoint: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 32% conversion through the final two-step sequence to the proline aminonitrile. This is not a measured yield of free proline. The sequence is represented as a composite reaction to avoid promoting a transient imine to an experimentally isolated intermediate. Sulfur redistribution and the S8 endmember remain formal bookkeeping rather than a measured coproduct inventory. No stereochemical bias is established.

reactions.name: Proposed acidic surface hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed, unvalidated screen: 0.1-10 mM aminonitrile, pH 0-1, and residence times from one day to several weeks in a shaded acidic geothermal pool. Test separate aliquots after photochemistry; directly acidifying the complete cyanide/sulfide broth is not assumed to be selective. A persistent strongly acidic reservoir, retention of the organic substrate and control of residual copper/sulfide are required. Quantify aminonitrile, intermediate prolinamide, free proline and decomposition products throughout.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed nitrile hydration followed by amide hydrolysis releases the carboxylic acid and ammonia/ammonium. Reference balance for an expected racemic precursor pool: 2 mol_014 + 4 mol_001 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 2 mol_004. Equal L and D coefficients specify the achiral-model expectation, not an experimentally measured enantiomeric ratio.
reactions.reasoning: Proposed extension, not a demonstrated continuation of the cited synthesis: Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminonitrile endpoint but do not provide a complete measured free-proline synthesis under this regime. Nitrile-to-amide-to-acid conversion is conventional chemistry, yet rates, retro-Strecker loss, substrate survival and free-proline recovery must be established for this specific compound and mixture. Strong acidity is a localized environmental assumption, not a generally available prebiotic reagent. This route is not ranked above alkaline or hydrothermal completion without comparative data.

reactions.name: Proposed alkaline surface hydrolysis of proline aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed, unvalidated screen: 0.1-10 mM aminonitrile, pH 10.5-11.5, and days-to-months residence in a shaded, locally alkaline evaporative or geothermal pool. Measure pH during evaporation rather than treating it as constant. Separate this prolonged processing stage from UV synthesis. Complete conversion cannot be assumed at these relatively moderate hydroxide activities; accumulation of prolinamide or decomposition instead of proline is a possible outcome.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-promoted nitrile hydration and subsequent amide hydrolysis produce prolinate and ammonia; the molecular node records the corresponding neutral reference composition. Reference balance: 2 mol_014 + 4 mol_001 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 2 mol_004.
reactions.reasoning: Proposed extension: the supplied research contains no substrate-specific validation of alkaline conversion of the Patel et al. (2015) proline aminonitrile under these conditions. A plausible reaction class does not establish an adequate environmental rate. Mildly alkaline processing may avoid requiring a concentrated acid reservoir, but potentially slow amide cleavage, competing reactions, dilution and long residence times remain serious limitations. No alkaline advantage or L-selectivity is claimed.

reactions.name: Proposed confined geothermal hydrolysis and rapid quench

conditions.temperature: 390-423 K during processing; quench below 330 K afterward
conditions.pressure: 10-30 bar, sufficient to retain liquid water
conditions.other: Proposed screen: 0.1-10 mM aminonitrile, approximately pH 6-8 at reaction temperature, and 0.5-24 hour residence times. Surface-derived precursor would need transport into shallow, confined geothermal fractures, not irradiation at depth. Determine precursor survival during transport. Quench the exiting fluid by rapid dilution or heat exchange, with a design target below 330 K within one minute. These residence and quench targets are proposed tests, not published proline production measurements.

reactions.mechanism: Thermally accelerated hydration and amide cleavage convert the nitrile into a carboxyl group. Reference balance: 2 mol_014 + 4 mol_001 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 2 mol_004. Cooling is a preservation operation, not a separate molecule-forming reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Proposed extension: Patel et al. (2015) do not demonstrate this hydrothermal completion. Bada et al. (1995) show why formation must be evaluated against irreversible thermal destruction, while Yanagawa and Kobayashi (1997) demonstrate that reducing conditions can affect amino-acid stability. Those studies do not supply rate constants for this particular aminonitrile. Moderate temperature and quenching are defensible design choices, but neither proves that hydrolysis outruns precursor and product destruction. No unspecified mineral catalyst is added.

reactions.name: Reducing atmospheric discharge generation and aqueous capture of HCN

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K in the receiving water; electrical discharge is a nonthermal energy source
conditions.other: Transient CH4/N2-rich reducing gas with water vapor and possible trace ammonia, coupled to a cooler aqueous receiver. Proposed receiver pH: 8.5-9.5 to aid cyanide retention. Capture and subsequently concentrate the aqueous cyanide fraction before supplying rxn_001, rxn_004 and rxn_008. No natural discharge duration, capture efficiency or millimolar cyanide inventory is established here. Sulfide-rich copper photochemistry is downstream, not assumed to occur inside the discharge apparatus.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical activation of carbon and nitrogen species produces HCN among a complex gas-phase network; water captures part of that inventory. Formal target-branch balance: 2 mol_017 + mol_018 -> 2 mol_002 + 3 mol_019. This equation is not a measured discharge product balance.
reactions.reasoning: Supported source class, with an inferred network coupling: Ring et al. (1972) establish productive reducing-gas discharge chemistry, and Rugheimer and Rimmer (2019) support atmospheric HCN availability more broadly through modeling. The particular coupling to the Patel et al. (2015) sequence is proposed, not experimentally integrated. Trail et al. (2011) argue against treating a globally persistent highly reducing atmosphere as the default, so this source is limited to localized or transient conditions. Its inclusion supplies an actual required reagent; it does not establish acetylene, ammonia, copper or sulfide co-availability.

reactions.name: Empirical reducing-gas discharge synthesis and recovery of proline
agents: Silicate reactor or shoreline interface, with catalytic contribution unresolved

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk water with a cooler condenser or receiving zone
conditions.catalyst: No deliberately added catalyst is required by the reported route; silicate surfaces may influence the product distribution
conditions.other: Reported feedstock family: CH4, N2, water and trace NH3 under electrical discharge. The supplied report does not specify an exact reproducible gas ratio, discharge dose or residence time, so none is presented as measured. A proposed comparison uses a days-long gas-water circulation experiment with matched silicate and inert-vessel controls. Separate unhydrolyzed and hydrolyzed analytical aliquots and use isotope-labeled feeds and blanks. Any strong-acid workup belongs to analytical recovery, not an assumed natural pond process.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical composite module: discharge-generated carbon/nitrogen intermediates undergo unresolved carbon-chain construction and pyrrolidine-ring formation, followed by analytical recovery. This is not encoded as an ordinary one-step Strecker mechanism. One balanced reference allocation is: 20 mol_017 + mol_018 + 2 mol_004 + 8 mol_001 -> 2 mol_015 + 2 mol_016 + 33 mol_019. The allocation does not identify actual nitrogen provenance, conversion or coproduct distribution.
reactions.reasoning: Direct endpoint evidence: Ring et al. (1972) detected proline, at approximately 1.5 micromoles, in a much larger amino-acid mixture. No substantial L-selectivity or resolved proline-specific mechanism was demonstrated. Criado-Reyes et al. (2021) show that silicate vessel composition can materially affect discharge chemistry, justifying an explicit surface-control requirement without assigning a proven proline-specific silicate catalyst. Trail et al. (2011) restrict the environmental interpretation to plausible transient or local reducing episodes. This supports laboratory recovery more strongly than a quantified natural proline flux.

reactions.name: Empirical thermal formaldehyde-ammonia synthesis followed by hydrolytic recovery

conditions.temperature: Approximately 458 K for the reported thermal synthesis; analytical hydrolysis is a separate subsequent operation
conditions.pressure: Confined aqueous synthesis; approximately 20-50 bar is a proposed retention envelope, not the reported reactor pressure
conditions.other: Reported observation: heating aqueous formaldehyde/ammonia near 185 C produces material that releases proline upon hydrolysis. The supplied report does not give exact feed concentrations or heating duration. A proposed implementation screen is 0.1-1 M formaldehyde and total ammonia, sampled over 1-24 hours, without claiming reproduction of the original yield. A separate proposed analytical reference is sealed 6 M HCl hydrolysis near 383 K for about 24 hours, with isotope tracing and reagent blanks; this is not asserted to be the original protocol or a naturally available workup.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical synthesis-and-workup module involving unresolved C-C construction, nitrogen incorporation, ring formation and hydrolysis of product material. No specific polymer or aminonitrile is invented. Formal reference balance: 12 mol_020 + 2 mol_004 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 2 mol_022 + 4 mol_001. Formic acid is a proposed oxidized-carbon balancing sink, not an established stoichiometric coproduct of the proline-producing branch.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysate endpoint evidence: Fox and Windsor (1970) reported proline after hydrolysis of heated formaldehyde/ammonia products. Wolman et al. (1971) and the historical hydrolysis-blank concerns summarized in the supplied research motivate stringent controls rather than dismissal of the result. No mineral catalyst is added because none is required by the reported recipe. The 458 K step requires confinement and cannot be assigned to an ordinary surface pool. The natural concentration mechanism, unresolved proline-bearing precursor and difference between analytical release and environmental free-proline availability remain major gaps.

reactions.name: Empirical formaldehyde-hydroxylamine multimetal-clay synthesis and hydrolytic recovery
agents: Molybdate at 0.1 mM as a selectivity-modifying component
Zn2+, Fe3+, Cu2+, Co2+ and Mn2+, each at approximately 0.1 mM in the laboratory reference medium

conditions.temperature: 373-383 K, corresponding to the reported 105 plus or minus 5 C synthesis
conditions.pressure: Sealed anoxic vessel; 2-5 bar is a proposed retention envelope, not a reported measured pressure
conditions.catalyst: Multicomponent metal-clay medium; no unique molybdate-only catalytic mechanism is established
conditions.other: Reported reference conditions: 0.30 M formaldehyde, 0.05 M hydroxylamine, initial pH 5.5, nitrogen atmosphere and seven days of heating. Select the reported 0.1 mM molybdate condition, not the 10 mM maximum-selectivity condition. Strong-acid analytical hydrolysis follows synthesis; a separate proposed reference workup is 6 M HCl near 383 K for about 24 hours, not asserted to be the original detailed protocol. This is a confined geothermal analogue because the temperature exceeds the specified ambient-pressure surface range. Trace Fe3+ is retained as a laboratory-medium component; no molecular oxygen or globally ferric environment is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical composite module: hydroxylamine/formaldehyde chemistry enters unresolved oxime, condensation and nitrogenous-product networks, with subsequent C5-ring formation and hydrolytic release. HCN involvement is possible but is not encoded as established. Formal reference balance: 14 mol_020 + 2 mol_021 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 4 mol_022 + 4 mol_001. Formic acid is an unverified redox-balancing allocation rather than a measured proline-branch coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysate endpoint and selectivity evidence: Hatanaka and Egami (1977) report approximately 0.16 mol% proline among analyzed amino-acid residues at 0.1 mM molybdate. The 2.75 mol% result belongs to 10 mM molybdate and is not transferred to this lower-Mo network. Scott et al. (2008) support strong caution about dissolved Mo availability in poorly oxygenated settings; even 0.1 mM requires a local enrichment explanation. Hydroxylamine supply and concentration are external assumptions. The exact ferric-containing multimetal recipe is a laboratory comparator: replacing Fe3+ with abundant environmental Fe2+ cannot be assumed to preserve the result. This route remains conditional rather than a demonstrated executable Hadean process.

reactions.name: Empirical reducing hydrothermal cyanide-formaldehyde-ammonium synthesis and recovery
agents: Pyrite-pyrrhotite-magnetite assemblage as a redox-buffering mineral system

conditions.temperature: Approximately 423 K synthesis, followed by quenching below 330 K
conditions.catalyst: Mineral redox-buffering assemblage; a proline-specific heterogeneous catalytic site is not established
conditions.other: Reported framework: concentrated cyanide/formaldehyde/ammonium solutions near 150 C and 10 bar with reducing mineral conditions. Because exact concentrations and residence times are not supplied in the report, a proposed test uses 0.1 M each of total cyanide, formaldehyde and ammonium, initial room-temperature pH 8-9, 1-5 bar H2 partial pressure within the total pressure budget, and 0.5-24 hour residence screens. These are design choices, not claimed original values or natural vent concentrations. H2 may be supplied locally by water-rock chemistry; the graph does not require transport of atmospheric H2 to a vent. Quench within a proposed one-minute target and analyze unhydrolyzed and hydrolyzed fractions separately.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical hydrothermal reaction network produces a proline-containing amino-acid mixture through unresolved chain assembly and ring closure. Ordinary Strecker chemistry alone is not asserted to explain the pyrrolidine ring. One formal reducing-branch balance is: mol_002 + 9 mol_020 + mol_004 + 3 mol_019 -> mol_015 + mol_016 + 5 mol_001. This is not a measured hydrogen consumption or product mass balance.
reactions.reasoning: Direct analytical endpoint evidence: Hennet et al. (1992) report proline under the stated hydrothermal framework and explicitly caution that their concentrated precursors were not claimed to represent natural fluids. Bada et al. (1995) require attention to thermal destruction, while Yanagawa and Kobayashi (1997) support considering hydrogen fugacity in preservation. Neither establishes net proline accumulation under the proposed residence-time screen. The mineral assemblage is justified as a redox/environmental control, not automatically as an isolated proline catalyst. Natural feedstock concentration, exact recovery conditions and synthesis-versus-destruction kinetics remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Supplied HCN to cyanosulfidic aminonitrile with acidic completion
pathways.description: Starts from supplied HCN, acetylene, ammonia, sulfide and water. Follows the experimentally supported ring-construction sequence and then the unvalidated acidic hydrolysis extension. L-proline is an expected component of the resulting DL mixture. This is a scaffold-supported pathway, not an experimentally completed environmental synthesis.

pathways.name: Supplied HCN to cyanosulfidic aminonitrile with alkaline completion
pathways.description: Shares the demonstrated scaffold chemistry of P1 but evaluates alkaline nitrile and amide hydrolysis in a separate, shaded surface compartment. Its distinction is the chemical product-release regime, not an independent ring-forming mechanism. Useful rates and survival under prolonged alkaline exposure remain unmeasured.

pathways.name: Supplied HCN to surface scaffold formation and confined geothermal completion
pathways.description: Builds the aminonitrile at the UV-exposed surface, then proposes transport into shallow confined geothermal water for hydrolysis and rapid quenching. Precursor transport, hydrolysis rates and thermal survival must all be demonstrated. This route is not claimed to outperform either surface hydrolysis option.

pathways.name: Discharge-supplied HCN feeding cyanosulfidic synthesis and acidic completion
pathways.description: Extends P1 upstream by generating and capturing HCN from methane/nitrogen discharge chemistry. Captured HCN supplies the multiple cyanide-requiring stages; acetylene, ammonia and sulfide remain separate feedstocks. This is an explicitly different feedstock-supply sequence, not a second experimental validation of the downstream scaffold or hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Discharge-supplied HCN feeding cyanosulfidic synthesis and alkaline completion
pathways.description: Combines explicit atmospheric cyanide supply with the scaffold sequence and the alkaline product-release test. Capture and concentration of atmospheric HCN are additional bottlenecks beyond those of P2. Neither the linked source-to-scaffold operation nor final free-proline yield has been demonstrated as one protocol.

pathways.name: Discharge-supplied HCN feeding surface scaffold formation and geothermal completion
pathways.description: Includes atmospheric HCN formation, surface aminonitrile assembly and proposed confined geothermal hydrolysis. It is a longer supply-and-processing variant of the same scaffold chemistry, not an independently demonstrated sixth proline synthesis. Both atmospheric capture and subsequent precursor transport require explicit flux and survival measurements.

pathways.name: Direct empirical reducing-atmosphere discharge family
pathways.description: Uses the Ring-type methane/nitrogen/water/trace-ammonia experiment as an empirical proline-producing module. Unlike P4-P6, it does not assume that the detected proline passed through the defined cyanosulfidic intermediates. The low-abundance endpoint, unresolved ring mechanism, vessel effects and transient reducing-atmosphere requirement are retained.

pathways.name: Thermal formaldehyde-ammonia synthesis with hydrolysate recovery
pathways.description: Represents formation of proline-releasing material from heated formaldehyde and ammonia, followed by analytical hydrolysis. The composite edge avoids inventing the uncharacterized precursor. Demonstrated laboratory recovery is distinguished from free-proline accumulation in a natural confined geothermal setting.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-hydroxylamine synthesis in the lower-molybdate multicomponent medium
pathways.description: Retains the experimentally observed hydrolysate route at 0.1 mM molybdate, without borrowing the 10 mM molybdate selectivity result. Hydroxylamine supply, local Mo enrichment, metal oxidation states, clay effects and strong-acid recovery remain unresolved environmental requirements. It is a conditional laboratory-supported family, not a validated natural reactor.

pathways.name: Reducing hydrothermal cyanide-formaldehyde-ammonium family
pathways.description: Represents the Hennet-type proline-producing hydrothermal network with explicit reducing mineral control and a proposed residence-time/quench screen. The empirical endpoint does not establish a unique ring-forming intermediate, natural precursor concentrations or an environmental free-proline flux. Locally supplied hydrothermal hydrogen is allowed without requiring an artificial cross-environment hydrogen transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest mechanistically resolved route. The scaffold sequence closely follows Patel et al. (2015), and acidic aminonitrile hydrolysis is chemically conventional. However, rxn_009 remains proposed rather than demonstrated under specified surface conditions. The supplied summaries also do not establish an uninterrupted synthesis through the separately optimized photochemical stages. Expected DL-proline formation includes the target L-enantiomer; lack of enantioenrichment is not itself a failure to produce L-proline as a mixture component.
suggestions: Specify the hydrolysis pH, temperature, duration and acid source, and measure aminonitrile-to-free-proline conversion under those conditions.
Test the staged sequence with realistic reagent carryover, including sulfide activity, irradiation exposure and copper speciation where copper is used.
Attach reaction-specific literature citations and quantify recovered proline, side products and enantiomeric composition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The experimentally supported scaffold provides a coherent precursor route. Alkaline nitrile hydrolysis is plausible, but rxn_010 lacks demonstrated conversion and selectivity within a specified surface operating window. Conversion through the amide intermediate, required reaction time and compatibility with the preceding mixture need verification. Strong-acid analytical recovery in other studies does not establish the effectiveness of this alkaline completion regime.
suggestions: Measure nitrile, amide and free-proline concentrations over time at explicitly stated alkaline pH and surface-compatible temperatures.
Identify a plausible source and buffering capacity for the required alkalinity.
Test hydrolysis in the actual photochemical product mixture rather than assuming results from purified precursor will transfer unchanged.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Surface scaffold formation followed by confined geothermal hydrolysis is chemically coherent, and rapid cooling is a physically sensible preservation strategy. The uncertainty is not the use of two environments, but whether transport and residence times permit hydrolysis before precursor or product destruction. The supplied summary does not provide the temperature, pressure, pH, flow rate or quench performance needed to establish that competition quantitatively.
suggestions: Measure hydrolysis and decomposition rates across the proposed temperature, pH and redox window.
Specify a physical transport mechanism into the confined heated zone, including dilution and adsorption losses.
Validate the proposed residence time and rapid quench in a flow experiment, measuring free proline before analytical hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Discharge generation of HCN is a credible upstream supply module, and its connection to the resolved cyanosulfidic branch is sensible. However, rxn_012 represents production and capture from a complex discharge mixture, not selective elementary conversion to pure HCN. The reducing gas regime, capture efficiency and delivered cyanide concentration remain unspecified. This pathway also inherits the unvalidated acidic completion in rxn_009.
suggestions: Specify the discharge gas composition, energy input and a justified local or transient reducing setting.
Quantify aqueous HCN capture, retention and concentration, including impurities that could affect downstream copper and sulfide chemistry.
Demonstrate acidic hydrolysis using aminonitrile produced from the captured discharge feed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sequence is structurally coherent and uses supported chemistry for atmospheric HCN generation and aminonitrile scaffold construction. Its principal unresolved interfaces are delivery of usable cyanide from the discharge mixture and effective alkaline hydrolysis of the final precursor. Atmospheric capture conditions and final hydrolysis conditions must be specified independently; suitable cyanide trapping does not automatically establish suitable aminonitrile hydrolysis.
suggestions: Document the composition and concentration of the captured cyanide solution entering rxn_001.
Specify the chemical changes between capture, photochemical processing and alkaline completion.
Measure free-proline recovery under the proposed alkaline conditions, including competing reactions and incomplete amide hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a plausible research sequence, but the atmospheric-capture interface and geothermal completion are not quantitatively integrated. The environmental concern is specific: precursor production, delivery, heated residence and cooling must collectively preserve enough material to yield free proline. Rapid quenching is a justified proposal, not evidence that the required hydrolysis and survival rates have been achieved.
suggestions: Develop a transport and reaction model covering HCN capture, scaffold formation, heated residence and cooling losses.
Test geothermal completion using the actual surface-generated precursor mixture.
Measure product survival under the proposed redox conditions rather than assuming reducing conditions or quenching are sufficient.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ring et al. (1972) provide direct experimental support for recovered proline from the stated reducing-gas family, although proline was a minor product and its ring-forming mechanism was unresolved. Encoding this as an empirical synthesis-and-recovery module is legitimate. Natural atmospheric applicability and surface effects remain uncertain. The balance solver's unequal L/D coefficients are only an algebraic solution and do not establish enantioselectivity or measured product proportions.
suggestions: Specify the reducing gas regime and reactor or mineral surfaces, accounting for the documented influence of silicate surfaces on discharge chemistry.
Report free proline before workup separately from total proline recovered after hydrolysis.
Use isotope tracing, procedural blanks and chiral analysis to establish product provenance and actual L/D recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Fox and Windsor (1970) support formation of material that releases proline after hydrolysis of thermal formaldehyde-ammonia products. Assigning the approximately 185 °C pressurized experiment to a hydrothermal thermal analogue is reasonable. The unidentified proline-releasing precursor and subsequent hydrolytic recovery prevent this from being a resolved environmental route to free proline. Formic acid makes the reference equation balanceable but is not an experimentally established coproduct inventory.
suggestions: Document thermal synthesis and hydrolytic recovery as separate operations without inventing structures for unidentified precursor material.
Specify pressure, reagent concentrations and retention conditions appropriate for the hot aqueous experiment.
Quantify pre-hydrolysis free proline and post-hydrolysis recovery using isotope-labeled feedstocks and hydrolysis blanks; test rather than assume the formic-acid coproduct.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hatanaka and Egami (1977) support this empirical proline-releasing reaction family. Choosing a lower-molybdate medium addresses an important critique, but the actual concentration must be stated: reported proline fractions were approximately 0.16 mol% at 10^-4 M molybdate and less than 0.01 mol% at 10^-6 M, not the 2.75 mol% observed at 10^-2 M. These are fractions of analyzed residues, not feedstock conversion yields. Concentrated organics, the multicomponent metal-clay medium and acid recovery remain environmental integration questions.
suggestions: Specify the selected molybdate concentration and associate it with the corresponding experimental product distribution.
Document hydroxylamine and formaldehyde activities, metal speciation, clay loading, sealed-vessel pressure and residence time.
Separate synthesis from hydrolytic recovery and measure absolute proline yield and coproducts, including whether formic acid is actually formed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hennet et al. (1992) provide empirical support for proline formation in reducing cyanide-formaldehyde-ammonium systems near 150 °C and 10 bar. The hydrothermal assignment is appropriate, and the module need not have an elementary mechanism to count as experimental endpoint evidence. Nevertheless, rxn_016 does not resolve ring construction, natural precursor activities or net product flux. Listing H2 alone does not establish the hydrogen fugacity needed to assess redox conditions and product survival.
suggestions: Specify pH, precursor concentrations, hydrogen fugacity and the actual mineral assemblage rather than relying on the hydrothermal label alone.
Measure proline formation and destruction as functions of residence time, followed by a quantified cooling or recovery operation.
Distinguish directly present free proline from any additional proline released during analytical workup.

evaluation.network_feedback: The complete network has sufficient molecule and reaction nodes, is connected, and uses molecule IDs consistently. The deterministic check establishes that all 16 reactions conserve atoms and charge with suitable coefficients; there are no conservation violations. S8-related coefficients and the solver's selected product ratios should not be interpreted as measured stoichiometry, yields or enantiomeric selectivity. Chemical and literature alignment are strongest for the resolved cyanosulfidic scaffold and for the experimentally observed proline endpoints of the four empirical modules. The network correctly distinguishes precursor synthesis, proposed hydrolysis and analytical recovery, and does not misrepresent P1-P6 as six independently demonstrated mechanisms. Nevertheless, acknowledging an unresolved operation does not validate it: the three aminonitrile hydrolysis regimes require direct testing, while the empirical modules need separately documented synthesis and recovery conditions. Detailed operating windows and reaction-specific citations are not present in the supplied reaction summaries. Environmental classifications are broadly reasonable, but reagent activities, catalyst speciation, physical transfers and formation-versus-destruction kinetics remain insufficiently constrained. Supplied feedstocks are legitimate boundary assumptions; their use is not itself a defect. Idealized sulfur and unverified formic-acid coproducts are acceptable conservation bookkeeping but do not establish actual reaction mechanisms or product inventories. Expected DL-proline production includes L-proline, so lack of enantioenrichment is not treated as failure to produce the target component; purified or preferentially produced L-proline is not demonstrated. Overall, this is a credible, evidence-graded research network, but not a sufficiently validated complete synthesis-and-recovery network to meet the 0.90 network approval threshold.
